description: GreenByte Explorers builds The Earth Information Jukebox for NASA Space Apps 2026: turning NASA Earth data into music to make climate science accessible. We seek teammates skilled or interested in coding, web development, data analysis, design, storytelling, and videography. No experience needed—just curiosity, reliability, and original work. Join us. We welcome all skill levels and backgrounds.
summary:
We developed the Earth Information Jukebox, a multi-sensory web application that addresses the challenge of making NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations accessible to everyone. NASA produces stunning visual data about our changing climate, but relying solely on sight limits accessibility for blind and low-vision individuals and makes complex data hard to connect with emotionally.

Our solution translates these visuals into sound through sonification. Using computer vision, the app analyzes NASA visual frames (from 2012-2023) to extract color, brightness, and pixel density. It then maps these metrics to musical frequencies—cool, low-density areas generate deep ambient tones, while warming, high-density areas generate urgent high frequencies. By turning visual climate data into immersive audio, the Jukebox makes Earth science inclusive, engaging, and accessible to all users.

Project Overview & Functionality:
The Earth Information Jukebox is a web application that transforms NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) data into immersive audio. Users select a year (2012-2023) and a dataset (such as Night Lights, Sea Surface Currents, or Lightning Events). The app uses computer vision (OpenCV) to analyze the selected NASA visual frame, extracting Average RGB, Brightness, and Pixel Density. It then maps these visual metrics to musical parameters: lower values (e.g., cool colors or sparse data) generate deep ambient tones (150-300 Hz), while higher values (warm colors or dense data) generate intense, urgent frequencies (500-800 Hz). By pressing "Play," users can hear the climate data translated into a real-time soundscape.

Impact & Benefits:
The primary goal is to bridge the accessibility gap in Earth science. By relying exclusively on visual charts, traditional climate data excludes blind and low-vision individuals. The Earth Jukebox makes complex data multi-sensory, allowing users to "hear" climate patterns and anomalies. It includes a "Screen Reader" mode that verbally announces the data, ensuring full accessibility. In the future, this tool can be integrated into educational platforms to teach climate change to visually impaired students, proving that critical scientific data isn't just for the eyes—it's for the ears.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend: React, Next.js
  • Data Processing: Python logic (OpenCV for image feature extraction)
  • Audio: Web Audio API
  • Hosting: Vercel

AI Disclosure:
In accordance with NASA guidelines, we utilized AI tools. We specifically used Claude AI and other LLMs to assist in generating foundational boilerplate code, debugging audio integration, and reviewing the project. We also used AI Text-to-Speech for our demo video voiceover due to the team lead's health constraints. All AI-generated logic was reviewed, customized, and rigorously tested by our team to fit the specific needs of the NASA dataset.

Creativity & Considerations:
Instead of building a traditional dashboard, we created a "Jukebox" interface, creatively mapping visual climate elements to musical notes to make science beautiful and accessible. Our team prioritized accessibility by designing a clean UI with large buttons and keyboard shortcuts. We strictly followed NASA's rules: no NASA logos were used, all NASA SVS datasets were properly credited, and all AI usage was transparently disclosed. We balanced strict data translation with musicality to ensure the output is both scientifically valid and pleasant to listen to.
